title: Traits (Interfaces)
intro: A trait is a list of methods a type promises to have. A trait can also include default methods, which a type gets without writing them. You use a trait to say what a function needs from its argument, instead of naming one type.

coming_from.go: A trait plays the part of a Go interface: the list of methods a function needs. The difference is that a type must say `impl Speaker for Robot`; having the right methods is not enough. A trait can also have default methods, which Go interfaces lack. And because the `impl` is a separate block, you can implement your own trait for types you did not write, such as `i32`, which Go does not allow.
coming_from.kotlin: A trait is close to a Kotlin interface with default methods. The `impl Speaker for Dog` block lives apart from the type, so you can implement your trait for types you did not write, like `i32`. A Kotlin extension function adds a method to such a type but does not make it a `Speaker`.
coming_from.python: A trait is like a `Protocol` with default methods, but a type counts only once you write `impl Speaker for Robot`, and the compiler checks it, not a separate type checker. (A default in a `Protocol` reaches only the classes that name it as a base.)
coming_from.typescript: A trait is like an `interface` plus the default method bodies you would otherwise put in an abstract class or a mixin. It's nominal, though: having a `speak` method isn't enough, the type must say `impl Speaker for Robot`.
coming_from.java: A `trait` is an `interface`, default methods included. A function that takes `&dyn Speaker` accepts any type that implements it, like a parameter of interface type, and `T: Speaker` is like `<T extends Speaker>`. The implementation lives in a separate `impl Speaker for Dog` block, so you can add your own trait to a type you didn't write, such as `String`, without a wrapper class.
coming_from.csharp: A `trait` is an `interface` with default methods. You implement it in a separate `impl Speaker for Robot` block, which means you can add your trait to someone else's type. A default method can be called on the type itself, where a C# default interface method is only visible through the interface type.
coming_from.c: C has no interfaces; you'd build a struct of function pointers by hand. A trait is that pattern written down for the compiler, which checks that every type fills in every method. Used as `&dyn Speaker`, it is a data pointer plus a pointer to such a table.
coming_from.cpp: A trait used through `&dyn Speaker` plays the part of an abstract base class with virtual methods, but a type does not inherit from it and a trait holds no data members. The same trait can also be a compile-time bound on a generic function, a lot like a C++20 concept, except that a type must say `impl Speaker for Robot`.

notes: `&dyn Speaker` means "a reference to some type that implements Speaker, decided at runtime". The right `speak` is looked up while the program runs.

There is also a compile-time version: `fn introduce(s: &impl Speaker)`. The compiler knows the exact type at each call, so it needs no lookup. Use `dyn` when you need a list of mixed types. The generics lesson covers the first, the trait objects lesson the second.
`format!` works like `println!`, but returns the text as a String instead of printing it.

gotcha.title: Having the method but not saying so
gotcha.looks_fine: In Go, Robot has a `Speak` method, so it is a Speaker automatically. Nothing else to write.
gotcha.rust_sees: Rust wants you to say it: `impl Speaker for Robot`. A method with a matching name is not enough.
gotcha.why: One type can then have two methods with the same name that mean different things: the lesson's `Car` has a `start` from `Vehicle` and another from `Appliance`, and a call says which. It also lets you add a trait to a type later, in a separate place, which is how `impl Speaker for i32` works.

go.says: Go runs this and prints beep 7. Having a `Speak` method is enough to count as a Speaker, with nothing to declare.

kotlin.says: Kotlin refuses this too: `Robot` has to declare `: Speaker` before it can be passed as one.
kotlin.error:
Main.kt:12:15: error: argument type mismatch: actual type is 'Robot', but 'Speaker' was expected.
    introduce(Robot(7))
              ^^^^^^^^

python.says: Python prints beep 7. Python uses duck typing: anything with a `speak` method works, with no need to declare that `Robot` is a Speaker.

typescript.says: Prints beep 7. TypeScript checks the shape: `Robot` has a matching `speak`, so it counts as a `Speaker` without saying `implements`.

java.says: Java refuses this too: `Robot` has a `speak` method but never says `implements Speaker`, so it is not a Speaker.
java.error:
Main.java:17: error: incompatible types: Robot cannot be converted to Speaker
        introduce(new Robot(7));
                  ^

csharp.says: C# refuses this too: having a Speak method is not enough, the class must say `: ISpeaker` (CS1503). Interfaces are opt-in by name in C#, as in Java.
csharp.error: Program.cs(1,11): error CS1503: Argument 1: cannot convert from 'Robot' to 'ISpeaker'

c.says: C has no traits or interfaces. A C "Speaker" is a struct of function pointers you fill in by hand, so there is no declaration to forget.

cpp.says: C++ refuses this too: `Robot` doesn't inherit from `Speaker`, so it can't be passed as a `const Speaker&`. A template or concept would accept it, since those only check that `speak()` exists.
